generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, every subject is a field of competing interpretations. A single piece of evidence can be read in more than one way, and scholarship advances when someone offers a reading others had not and defends it. Creativity here is disciplined imagination: holding rival interpretations of a source in tension rather than adopting the most cited, and placing your own reading among them with reasons.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students discussing the same influential source on their shared reading list.

Student A summarises the source faithfully and treats it as settled: this is what the literature says, so this is the position to adopt. The reading is accurate, but it is closed. No other interpretation is admitted, and Student A's own voice never enters; the discourse is reported, not opened. This is interpretation treated as a fixed account.

Student B reads the same source as one interpretation among several. Student B asks what each rival reading assumes and what it leaves out, then advances a reading of their own, argued from the evidence and placed explicitly against the others. This is interpretation treated as creative and contestable.

Both understood the source. Only Student B opened up the discourse and justified a voice of their own within the debate.
generatedProse.summary: Creativity in scholarship is disciplined imagination: reading a source as one contestable interpretation, opening up the discourse around it, and justifying a reading of your own against the evidence and the alternatives. You can now critique how creativity features in interpretation, appraise an interpretation by opening up its discourse, and defend your own voice in a debate. With the earlier lessons, you can treat creativity as a professional attribute, a mode of self-regulation, and a scholarly practice.

check.body: You are writing about a key source in your field. Which approach best justifies your own reading as one creative voice in the debate?

items.text: Set the source against rival interpretations and argue your reading from the evidence.
Adopt the source's interpretation because it is the most cited.
Summarise the source as accurately as possible and add nothing further.
Assert your reading strongly without reference to other interpretations.

feedback.correct: That's right. You justify your reading by placing it against rivals and arguing from evidence.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that argues your reading against other interpretations.
feedback.incorrectFinal: A reading is justified by setting it against rivals and arguing from evidence. Deference, bare summary and assertion do not.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
